newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - Kohl confident on punctual EMU, recovery.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Kohl confident on punctual EMU, recovery.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl left no room for doubt on Thursday that Germany would do its utmost to make the grade for Europe's single currency, insisting it will be launched on time in 1999.

In an interview from his Easter holiday retreat in Austria with ARD television, Kohl sought to dispel any doubt about Germany's ability to meet the tough fiscal criteria for entry into European economic and monetary union (EMU).

He recognised it would be "extremely difficult" to both fulfil the criteria and stick to the timetable. But when asked whether EMU would be delayed beyond 1999 should Germany fail to keep its deficit within the allowed limit of three percent of gross domestic product, he said: "We will achieve both -- this number is what counts."

The Maastricht Treaty on EMU sets limits on a range of economic targets, including budget deficits and total public debt, that countries must meet this year in order to qualify for monetary union in 1999. The participants in the first wave of EMU are expected to be chosen early next year.

Germany failed to meet the Maastricht deficit goal last year and economists and Bundesbank officials have warned that it could fail to meet the target again this year, giving rise to speculation that EMU, which is unthinkable without Germany, could be delayed.

One of the main obstacles to lowering the budget deficit is Germany's record unemployment, at its highest level since 1933. But Kohl said there was a good chance that jobless levels would "flatten out slightly" this year.
The economy, emerging from a period of weakness, was set to expand between two percent and 2.5 percent this year, he said.
Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said they would not approve a revision of proposed additions to the Maastricht Treaty unless they contained a strong commitment to fighting unemployment.

Heide Wieczorek-Zeul, the party's European affairs spokeswoman, said Kohl's government was trying to water down a new draft, due to be adopted by European Union leaders at an Amsterdam summit in June.
"The SPD will not approve the ratification of the revised ...treaty without the obligation of EU member states to an active employment policy," she told a news conference.
Wieczorek-Zeul also slammed Finance Minister Theo Waigel for linking cuts in social spending with the need to meet the criteria for EMU.
"This pulls the support of the population away from European unity," she said. "Nothing is forcing the government to pursue its failed tax and finance policies except its own neoliberal dogma."
Kohl dismissed opposition demands that he meet SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine as a precondition to resuming cross-party talks on tax cuts and other social welfare reforms.

"Why should I talk to Lafontaine? We already have working groups on tax reform," he said, adding that Lafontaine was only seeking to improve his own political profile ahead of next year's general elections.
"We have considerable problems in this country and it does not matter whether two people sit down together," Kohl said.

Kohl also said the government would move forward with reforms in other areas such as social welfare, health, and that a proposed "Family Fund" to help ease the burdens on the pension system would be established.
He acknowleged that financing the fund through increases in indirect taxes such value added and petrol taxes was being considered.
Kohl also urged the SPD to stop blocking the reforms and said opposition criticism of the government programme was drawn from the "dustbin of Marxist thought".
